# Bioresorbable Vascular Scaffolds in Percutaneous Coronary Intervention: Evolution, Pitfalls, and Next-Generation Horizons

### Introduction and Historical Context
Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has undergone several revolutions, from plain old balloon angioplasty to bare-metal stents and permanent metallic drug-eluting stents (DES). While contemporary DES have significantly reduced restenosis and stent thrombosis, they permanently cage the coronary artery, which limits long-term vasomotion, prevents positive vascular remodeling, and poses a lifelong risk of very late adverse events. The concept of "vascular restorative therapy" was introduced to address these limitations by providing transient mechanical support and drug delivery, followed by complete resorption, eventually leaving a native, fully functional vessel behind. 

The earliest clinical feasibility of this concept was demonstrated by the non-drug-eluting poly-L-lactic acid (PLLA) Igaki-Tamai scaffold [1], which showed favorable long-term safety over a decade [2]. This paved the way for first-generation drug-eluting polymeric scaffolds, led by the everolimus-eluting Absorb BVS (Abbott Vascular) [3]. Early clinical trials (ABSORB Cohort A and B) confirmed the feasibility of this technology, showing complete scaffold resorption within three years accompanied by restored vasomotion and late luminal enlargement [4, 5].

### The Polymeric Era: Hopes, Trials, and Clinical Downfall
Based on encouraging early-phase data, the Absorb BVS was rapidly adopted in clinical practice. Initial randomized controlled trials, such as the ABSORB II trial [6] and the ABSORB III trial [8], demonstrated that the scaffold was non-inferior to the cobalt-chromium everolimus-eluting stent (CoCr-EES; Xience) in terms of target lesion failure (TLF) at one year. However, as long-term follow-up data accumulated, a significant safety signal emerged. The 3-year results of ABSORB II [7] and the 3-year and 5-year results of ABSORB III [9, 10] revealed a troubling trend: a statistically significant increase in late target vessel myocardial infarction (TVMI) and very late scaffold thrombosis (ScT) compared to metallic DES. 

This was further corroborated by the investigator-initiated, all-comers AIDA trial, which reported a four-fold increase in scaffold thrombosis at two years [11], a safety concern that persisted up to the final five-year follow-up [12]. To address these concerns under optimized conditions, the ABSORB IV trial was conducted, mandating the exclusion of small vessels and suggesting post-dilatation [13]. Despite these procedural improvements, the 5-year clinical results of ABSORB IV still did not demonstrate superiority or overcome the early thrombotic hazard of first-generation polymeric scaffolds [14]. 

Large pooled individual-patient-data meta-analyses, including 1-year [15], 2-year [16], 3-year [17], and 5-year [18] follow-ups, confirmed that the first-generation polymeric scaffold was associated with elevated risks of TLF and scaffold thrombosis, especially driven by the treatment of very small target vessels, as highlighted in comprehensive systematic reviews [19].

### Mechanisms of Failure and the Implantation Protocol
The pathobiology of polymeric scaffold failure is multi-faceted. Intracoronary imaging and histopathological studies of failed scaffolds identified several core culprits: the extreme thickness of the PLLA struts (150 µm compared to 81 µm for Xience), which caused flow disturbances and platelet activation [22]; late structural discontinuities during the resorption process [23]; and the development of neoatherosclerosis within the scaffolded segment [24]. Additionally, suboptimal deployment—such as incomplete strut apposition and underexpansion—was heavily implicated in both early and late thrombotic events [23].

These findings led to the development of the protocolized "PSP" approach (Prepare the lesion, Size the scaffold correctly using quantitative coronary angiography or intravascular imaging, and Post-dilate with non-compliant balloons) [20]. Clinical and post-hoc analyses of the ABSORB trials confirmed that strict adherence to the PSP technique significantly minimized the risk of scaffold thrombosis, particularly when avoiding vessels under 2.25 mm [21]. However, despite technique optimization, the intrinsic mechanical limitations of thick polymer struts remained a hurdle.

### The Resorbable Metallic Paradigm and Future Directions
The drawbacks of polymeric scaffolds spurred interest in alternative materials, particularly bioresorbable magnesium alloys, which offer superior tensile strength and allow for thinner struts. The first-in-man BIOSOLVE-I trial demonstrated the feasibility of the early-generation drug-eluting absorbable metal scaffold (DREAMS) [25]. This was succeeded by the sirolimus-eluting Magmaris scaffold (DREAMS 2G), which featured a 120 µm strut thickness and a resorption time of approximately 12 months [26]. Long-term five-year data from the BIOSOLVE-II trial confirmed the sustained safety and performance of this magnesium-based platform [27].

Crucially, preclinical evaluations in porcine models demonstrated that the magnesium platform is significantly less thrombogenic than its polymeric counterpart, exhibiting a thrombogenicity profile comparable to that of permanent metallic DES [28]. The safety of Magmaris in broader clinical scenarios has been validated in the large-scale BIOSOLVE-IV registry, showing reassuring safety and performance up to two years [29]. Ultimately, next-generation bioresorbable scaffolds seek to prove their clinical utility and establish whether they can successfully compete with modern DES [30]. Thinner struts, hybrid alloy-polymer designs, and routine intravascular imaging-guided deployment represent the pathways through which bioresorbable vascular scaffolds may successfully reclaim a central role in percutaneous coronary interventions.
